body:
## Module 8 in two minutes

Seven modules were about control. This one is about what it was for — and the question it won't let you avoid is **where the capacity goes**, because capacity nobody assigns doesn't stay capacity. It dissipates, and then gets counted as a saving anyway.

The most instructive thing in the field is a reversal. In **2023** IBM's CEO said AI would replace thousands of back-office roles and froze back-office hiring. The company then built one of the best HR service deployments in existence — the AskHR agent this track cites twice. In **February 2026** it announced it was **tripling entry-level hiring**, across engineering and HR, with its CHRO's reasoning stated plainly: stop investing in juniors and in three to five years there is no pipeline. The jobs were rewritten rather than removed. Total employment went up.

**The obvious reading is wrong.** This isn't automation failing — AskHR works. It's what happened to the capacity:

> **Capacity you don't deliberately redeploy gets stranded — and the pipeline is the first thing you lose and the last thing you can rebuild.**

So name where it goes **inside the enablement decision**, at the same time, in the same document. "Redeployed to higher-value work" means nobody has decided, and it will still mean that in eighteen months.

### Where the agent goes on the chart

A question you'll be asked and nobody else in People can answer, because it's a configuration decision in a system you administer. And it's already live: in a mid-2026 survey of 1,200+ managers and executives, about **31% said leadership is framing AI as a teammate or employee**, and nearly one in four said agents are formally on org or workflow charts.

**The emerging convention is the right one, and you've already built it:** an agent is not a person and occupies no headcount box. What goes on the chart is **the accountable human owner** — every agent reports to a named person who answers for its outputs. That is Module 1's accountability column and Module 7's signature, arriving from the org-design direction. **The chart question resolves into the register question.**

Four consequences that are yours. **Don't create worker records for agents** — it breaks headcount and every ratio derived from it, and creates a person-shaped object with no employment relationship. **Do record the agent as an asset with an owner**, probably not in the HCM. **Do decide what happens when the owner leaves**, because that's the offboarding cascade with a new node. And **notice what breaks in reporting**: if work moved to agents and your denominators didn't change, span of control and cost per employee now measure something different from last year — and nobody will announce it.

**Every track in this curriculum closes on a bet with three terms** — which change, what you'd measure at 90 days, what you'd stop doing to fund it. **You get a fourth, and it's yours alone: what would you turn off?**

No other role can subtract. An HRBP can't retire a process; a recruiter can't disable an integration. You can — and it's often the better bet, because **every capability you turn off is one that no longer has to be reviewed, measured, logged for six months, disclosed, consulted on, or signed for.** The first candidate is usually sitting in your register: the widest-reach capability with no named owner. Nobody will fight for it, precisely because nobody owns it.

Then the test that separates the two things this module is about: **is there a state of the world in which you do not proceed?** If the vendor is signed, the date is in the newsletter and the training is built, you're describing a migration. That may be right — but call it one, because using "bet" for something that can't go either way is how a function loses the ability to stop anything.

**And the seat you already have.** HR has no direct involvement in AI strategy in 52% of organizations — while its technology function is the second-most-adopted area in HR. So the function is excluded from the strategy conversation and **its systems are where the AI actually runs.** You're in every implementation conversation, with artifacts nobody else can produce. Not the back office: **the control surface.** Every other track ends by telling its learner to find out who the deployer is. You're the answer.
